# Measurements that have not finished

Incremental estimation over a growing record, and dynamic stability.

## `stabilis.stream`

Measurements that are still running, and records that are not stationary.

Everything else in this library takes a finished record and asks what it
is worth. This package covers the two questions that arrangement cannot
answer.

**"What is it doing right now?"** -- `source.py` and `collect.py` bring
samples in from a file being appended to, a socket, or an array being
replayed, and `online.py` maintains the overlapping Allan variance in
O(max τ) memory as they arrive. The acceptance test is an identity, not a
comparison: replay a record through the streaming path and it must give
back what the batch estimator gives, which is why this package was built
after the batch core was validated rather than before. Measured, the two
agree to 2 ulp -- and the residual is the batch path's pairwise summation
error, since the accumulator's sum is compensated and the coefficients are
bit-identical.

**"Was it doing the same thing all along?"** -- `davar.py` evaluates any
registered estimator over a sliding window, giving σ(τ, t) as a surface.
A warm-up, a bump, an air conditioner cycling: all of them are invisible
in a single σ(τ) curve, which averages them into the answer, and obvious
as a ridge in the surface. `davar(x, window=len(x))` returns bit for bit
what the batch call returns, because it *is* the batch call.

The rule shared by both halves, and the reason `collect.py` is longer than
the arithmetic it contains: **a sample that never arrived becomes a NaN in
its own slot, never the disappearance of a slot.** Appending arriving
samples to a list is the natural implementation and it is wrong in the
worst possible way -- a dropped reading shifts the whole timebase after it
and makes the record look *better*, with no symptom anywhere.

Nothing here is re-exported at the top level of `stabilis`. Realtime work
is a different mode of use from analysing a file, and `from stabilis.stream
import davar` says which mode you are in.

Re-exports: `replay`, `tail_file`, `tcp_lines`, `udp_lines`, `parse_lines`, `grid_slot`, `on_grid`, `collect`, `feed`, `GRID_TOLERANCE`, `MAX_GAP_SAMPLES`, `OnlineAvar`, `online_avar`, `online_push`, `online_push_many`, `online_result`, `MAX_RING_BYTES`, `DavarSurface`, `davar`, `MAX_WINDOWS`, `STEP_DIVISOR`.

## `stabilis.stream.collect`

Putting arriving samples back on the grid they were sampled on.

Everything in `stats/` assumes a uniform timebase: `x[i]` is the phase at
`epoch + i/rate_hz`, and every estimator's second difference is a
statement about three samples a fixed number of slots apart. A stream
arrives as `(t, value)` pairs and has no such guarantee, so the whole job
of this module is one rule:

**A sample that never arrived becomes a NaN in its own slot. It never
becomes the disappearance of a slot.**

Getting that wrong is the worst available failure mode, because it is
invisible. Append arriving samples to a list and a counter that dropped
fifty readings hands you a record that is fifty samples shorter and
*perfectly smooth*: every later sample has slid earlier by fifty
intervals, the timebase is wrong from the outage onward, and σ_y(τ) comes
back looking better than the oscillator is. Placing samples by timestamp
instead makes the outage a gap, which the estimators already handle
honestly (`theory/gaps.md`) and which shows up in `n_gaps` and in
provenance.

The three things `on_grid` refuses, rather than repairing:

* **A timestamp that is not near a grid slot.** Off by more than a
  quarter of a sample and the declared rate is not the rate the data was
  taken at. Interpolating onto the declared grid would be inventing data;
  the correct response is to say so and let the caller fix the rate.
* **A timestamp that goes backwards, or repeats one already placed.**
  Sorting it into position would mean taking the record's order from the
  network's scheduling rather than from the instrument.
* **A gap longer than `max_gap` slots.** An hour's outage at 1 MHz is
  three billion NaNs, and materializing them is not a service to anybody.

`parse_lines` is the text half: it turns lines into `(t, value)` pairs and
carries the one honest warning of the module -- a file with no timestamp
column *cannot* tell you a sample went missing, so its gaps are
undetectable by construction, and that fact goes into provenance rather
than being left for a reader to work out.

#### `GRID_TOLERANCE`

```python
GRID_TOLERANCE = 0.25
```

How far from a grid slot a timestamp may land, in samples. A quarter of an interval is well past any plausible logging jitter and well short of the half-sample at which the assignment becomes ambiguous.

#### `MAX_GAP_SAMPLES`

```python
MAX_GAP_SAMPLES = 1 << 20
```

Longest run of missing samples that will be materialized as NaN.

#### `parse_lines`

```python
parse_lines(lines, column: int=0, time_column: int | None=None, rate_hz: float | None=None, epoch: float=0.0, delimiter: str | None=None, gap_value: float | None=None)
```

Turn text lines into `(t, value)` pairs, skipping comments and blanks.

With `time_column` set, `t` comes from the file. Without it, `t` is
synthesized as `epoch + i/rate_hz` from the arrival order -- which is
the common case for a logger that just prints numbers, and which means
**a dropped sample is undetectable**: the line that would have carried
it is simply not there, and nothing in the remaining text says so. That
is a property of the data, not a limitation here, but it is the reason
`collect` records which of the two it used.

A line that does not parse is skipped rather than fatal; a live feed
that dies on one malformed line from a counter's startup banner is
worse than one that ignores it.

#### `grid_slot`

```python
grid_slot(t: float, epoch: float, rate_hz: float) -> tuple[int, float]
```

Which grid slot a timestamp belongs in, and how far off it landed.

    slot = (t - epoch) * rate_hz
    index = round(slot);  offset = slot - index      [samples]

Returned as a pair because the offset is the only diagnostic that
cannot be recovered once the sample is placed: a record whose samples
all sit 0.2 of an interval late was taken at a different rate from the
one declared, and after placement it looks perfect.

#### `on_grid`

```python
on_grid(pairs, rate_hz: float, epoch: float, tolerance: float=GRID_TOLERANCE, max_gap: int=MAX_GAP_SAMPLES, start_index: int=0)
```

Place `(t, value)` pairs on the grid, filling missing slots with NaN.

Yields `(index, value, offset)` for every slot from `start_index`
onward, in order and with no slot skipped. `offset` is the arriving
sample's fractional grid error in samples, and NaN for a slot that was
filled rather than received.

`start_index` is for resuming a feed: an accumulator that has already
absorbed `k` samples must be handed slot `k` next, and a stream whose
first timestamp lands earlier than that is a caller error rather than
something to reconcile.

#### `collect`

```python
collect(pairs, rate_hz: float, kind: str='phase', epoch: float | None=None, source: str='stream', tolerance: float=GRID_TOLERANCE, max_gap: int=MAX_GAP_SAMPLES, timestamps: bool=True)
```

Drain a stream into a `PhaseSeries` or `FreqSeries`.

`epoch` defaults to the first timestamp seen, which is what makes the
result's phase offsets small (see `theory/precision.md`). Pass one
explicitly to place a stream on a grid that started earlier -- the
leading slots come back as gaps, correctly.

`timestamps=False` records that the timestamps were synthesized from
arrival order rather than measured, which is what `parse_lines` does
for a file with no time column. The samples land in the same places
either way; what changes is the claim the record may make, so it goes
into provenance and the gap count is reported as *detected* rather than
complete.

#### `feed`

```python
feed(acc: OnlineAvar, pairs, epoch: float | None=None, tolerance: float=GRID_TOLERANCE, max_gap: int=MAX_GAP_SAMPLES) -> OnlineAvar
```

Push a stream through the grid and into an online accumulator.

The same placement `collect` does, without ever holding the record:
memory stays at the accumulator's `2*max(m)+1` samples however long the
measurement runs. Resumable -- feeding a second stream continues from
the slot after the last one absorbed, so the two together give exactly
what one uninterrupted feed would.

`epoch` defaults to the accumulator's, which is the right default when
resuming and the right one on the first call if `online_avar` was told
the epoch. Falling back to the first timestamp would put a resumed feed
on a fresh grid and silently discard the outage between them.

## `stabilis.stream.davar`

The dynamic Allan variance: σ_y(τ) as a function of when you looked.

Every statistic in `stats/` returns one number per τ for a whole record,
which presumes the record is stationary. A real oscillator is not: it
warms up, it gets bumped, its enclosure's air conditioning cycles, the GPS
antenna sees a different sky. Galleani and Tavella's DAVAR is the obvious
repair -- evaluate the same estimator over a window and slide the window
along the record, giving a surface σ_y(τ, t) whose ridges are the events.

**It is computed by recomputing, not by sliding.** The literature's update
form adds the entering term and subtracts the expiring one, which is O(1)
per step and loses significance without bound: subtractive cancellation in
a running sum of squares has no self-correcting mechanism, and on a long
record the surface drifts away from the truth in a way that looks like a
physical trend. Direct recomputation over the existing estimator costs
`window/step` times one batch call, which for any window worth plotting is
a fraction of a second -- and it buys two things worth more than the
speed:

* **`davar(x, window=len(x))` is bit-identical to the batch call**, not
  equal to 1e-15. Same code path, same data, same rounding. That identity
  is the acceptance test for this module, and it exists only because
  nothing here reimplements the estimator.
* **Every estimator comes free.** The surface is built by name through the
  registry, so `kind="ohdev"` gives a dynamic Hadamard deviation and a
  third-party plugin gets a dynamic form without writing any code.

Two honesty rules the surface follows:

* **Only whole windows.** A truncated window at either end has fewer
  terms, a shorter longest τ and a different EDOF, so plotting it beside
  the others draws an edge artefact that reads as a physical transient.
  The uncovered half-window at each end is reported rather than filled.
* **A τ a window cannot estimate is NaN, not omitted.** Gaps shorten a
  window's longest contiguous run, so the same τ may be available in one
  window and not the next. Dropping it would make the surface ragged;
  filling it would invent a number. NaN is the third option and the only
  correct one.

#### `MAX_WINDOWS`

```python
MAX_WINDOWS = 2048
```

Ceiling on how many windows one call may evaluate. Each is a full batch run, so the cost is linear in this and a default `step` on a long record can ask for a great many. The message names `step`, which is the knob.

#### `STEP_DIVISOR`

```python
STEP_DIVISOR = 10
```

Default `step`, as a fraction of the window. Ten steps per window resolves an event to a tenth of the averaging span, which is as fine as the surface means anything: two windows overlapping by 90 % share 90 % of their terms and cannot disagree by much.

#### `DavarSurface`

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DavarSurface
```

σ²(τ, t) on a rectangular grid of averaging factors and window times.

`var` is `(n_windows, n_taus)`, NaN where that window could not
estimate that τ. `t_s` is the *centre* time of each window in the
original series' timebase, which is where an event the window
straddles actually happened.

*Fields*

```python
kind: str
af: np.ndarray
tau_s: np.ndarray
t_s: np.ndarray
start_index: np.ndarray
var: np.ndarray
n_terms: np.ndarray
window: int
step: int
rate_hz: float
epoch: float
scale: float
provenance: Provenance
var_lo: np.ndarray | None = None
var_hi: np.ndarray | None = None
level: float | None = None
edof: np.ndarray | None = None
span_factor: int = 2
is_variance: bool = True
```

*property* `dev(self) -> np.ndarray`

The deviation surface, `sqrt(var)`. NaN stays NaN.

*property* `n_windows(self) -> int`

*method* `window_result(self, k: int) -> StabilityResult`

One window as an ordinary `StabilityResult`, for plotting or export.

*method* `at_af(self, af: int) -> np.ndarray`

The time series of `var` at one averaging factor.

#### `davar`

```python
davar(series: PhaseSeries | FreqSeries, window: int, step: int | None=None, taus='octave', kind: str='oadev', max_af: int | None=None, gap_policy: str='auto', level: float | None=None, method: str='auto', max_windows: int=MAX_WINDOWS) -> DavarSurface
```

Evaluate `kind` over sliding windows of `window` samples.

    starts   = 0, step, 2*step, ...  while start + window <= n
    var[k]   = kind(series[start_k : start_k + window])

`window` is in **samples**, not seconds, because it has to be an
integer number of slots for the τ grid to be the same in every window,
and rounding a duration to samples silently is how two runs of the same
analysis end up on different grids.

`step` defaults to `window // STEP_DIVISOR` and is recorded. `level`,
if given, computes a confidence interval per window while its
coefficients still exist -- there is no way to add one afterwards.

Passing `window = series.n` gives exactly one window and returns, bit
for bit, what calling `kind` on the whole record returns. That is
tested, and it is the reason the surface is built this way.

## `stabilis.stream.online`

The overlapping Allan variance, maintained one sample at a time.

A live measurement has no length, so nothing here may touch the whole
record. What it keeps instead is one running sum of squared coefficients
per averaging factor, plus the last `2*max(m)+1` phase samples, and that
is enough: every term the batch estimator forms is formed here exactly
once, when its last sample arrives.

    d[i] = x[i+2m] - 2*x[i+m] + x[i]

is a function of three samples, so at sample index `k` the term ending
there is `d = (x[k] - 2*x[k-m]) + x[k-2m]` -- written in that association
order deliberately, because it is the order `numpy` uses to evaluate the
batch expression in `stats/classical.py`, and matching it makes every
coefficient bit-identical rather than merely close.

**What is therefore *not* bit-identical is the sum**, and that is the only
difference between the two paths. `np.mean` sums pairwise; an accumulator
cannot, because it never sees more than one term at a time. So the sum
here is Neumaier-compensated, which makes it the *more* accurate of the
two -- the residual disagreement is the batch estimator's pairwise error,
not ours. `theory/stream.md` carries the measured figure.

**This is the one mutable container in the library.** Returning a fresh
frozen dataclass per sample would allocate once per sample, which at a
counter's output rate is the whole cost of the thing. It has no methods,
and every function that touches it is a plain function below, so the
"frozen dataclasses for data, functions for behaviour" rule still holds in
the only way that matters: nothing here is polymorphic.

#### `MAX_RING_BYTES`

```python
MAX_RING_BYTES = 1 << 28
```

Ceiling on the phase history one accumulator may hold. The ring is `2*max(af)+1` float64, so this is a direct bound on the largest averaging factor a stream may track -- about 16 million at the default. It is a memory bound rather than a preference, and it is stated because the alternative is a process killed by the allocator, which is not an error the code gets to report.

#### `OnlineAvar`

```python
@dataclass
class OnlineAvar
```

Running state for the overlapping Allan variance of one channel.

Mutable, and mutated in place by `online_push`. See the module
docstring for why. Nothing outside this module should assign to a
field; read them freely.

*Fields*

```python
rate_hz: float
tau0: float
af: np.ndarray
epoch: float
provenance: Provenance
ring: np.ndarray
total: np.ndarray
comp: np.ndarray
count: np.ndarray
n_seen: int = 0
n_gaps: int = 0
```

#### `online_avar`

```python
online_avar(rate_hz: float, af, epoch: float=0.0, source: str='stream') -> OnlineAvar
```

Start an accumulator for the averaging factors `af`.

The averaging factors are **explicit and required**. A batch estimator
derives its tau grid from the record length; a stream has no length, so
deriving one would mean guessing how long the measurement will run and
then either wasting memory or silently capping the longest tau. Naming
them is the honest form of that decision, and `tau.suggest(n)` will
name a grid for an expected `n` if the caller wants one.

#### `online_push`

```python
online_push(acc: OnlineAvar, value: float) -> OnlineAvar
```

Absorb one phase sample. Returns the same accumulator, for chaining.

    k = n_seen
    for each m with k >= 2m:
        d = (x[k] - 2*x[k-m]) + x[k-2m]
        c = d / (m * tau0)
        total[m] += c**2  (compensated);  count[m] += 1

A NaN sample is stored like any other, so it spoils exactly the terms
whose window contains it and no others -- the same arithmetic the batch
`gap_policy="mask"` path does, reached by the same route rather than by
a second rule.

#### `online_push_many`

```python
online_push_many(acc: OnlineAvar, values) -> OnlineAvar
```

Absorb a chunk of samples, in order. Identical to pushing one by one.

Chunking is an ingest convenience -- a socket read returns whatever
arrived -- and must never change the answer, so this really is the loop
and not a second implementation of it.

#### `online_result`

```python
online_result(acc: OnlineAvar) -> StabilityResult
```

The overlapping Allan deviation implied by the stream so far.

    var[m] = scale * ( (total[m] + comp[m]) / count[m] ),  scale = 1/2

Cheap and repeatable: call it after every sample if you want a live
trace. Averaging factors that have not yet seen a complete term are
absent from the result rather than present and zero.

`coeffs` is empty, and permanently so -- retaining the coefficient
arrays is the one thing an O(m) accumulator cannot do. `confidence()`
therefore refuses this result, which is correct: the data-driven EDOF
it would want is a function of the coefficients it does not have. Use
`davar` over the collected record, or collect and re-run in batch, when
an interval is needed.

## `stabilis.stream.source`

Where live samples come from. Generators, not classes.

A source is a generator. That is the whole abstraction: no base class, no
`start`/`stop`/`read` protocol, no object to keep alive. `for line in
tail_file(path):` is the interface, `break` is the shutdown, and a
generator that has been closed has released its socket or file handle
because `finally` ran. Anything a class would have carried -- partial-line
buffering, reconnect, idle timeout -- is local state in exactly one
function.

Two shapes live here and they are deliberately different.

* **`replay` yields `(t, value)` pairs**, because it already knows both.
  It is the source the test suite runs on, and the one that makes the
  streaming path checkable at all: replaying a record and analysing the
  same record in batch must agree, which is an identity rather than a
  comparison.
* **`tail_file`, `tcp_lines` and `udp_lines` yield text lines**, because
  a byte stream does not know what a sample is. Turning a line into a
  `(t, value)` pair is `collect.parse_lines`, which is where the column
  layout and the missing-timestamp question belong.

`serial` is not here. It needs `pyserial` and, more to the point, hardware
to test against; shipping an untested source and listing it in the feature
table is how a library acquires a function nobody has ever run. It arrives
with the first instrument.

#### `READ_BYTES`

```python
READ_BYTES = 1 << 16
```

One read from a file or socket. Small enough that a slow trickle is not held back waiting for a buffer to fill, large enough that a fast one is not a syscall per sample.

#### `replay`

```python
replay(values, rate_hz: float, epoch: float=0.0, skip_gaps: bool=False)
```

Replay an array as a timestamped stream on a perfect grid.

    t[i] = epoch + i / rate_hz

`skip_gaps` is the interesting flag: with it set, a non-finite entry is
**not emitted at all**, which is what a counter does when it fails to
produce a reading. The timestamps of everything after it are unchanged,
so the only evidence a sample went missing is the jump in `t` -- and
reconstructing it is `collect.on_grid`'s job. Turning that flag on and
getting the same answer back is the test that the ingest path does not
silently renumber.

#### `tail_file`

```python
tail_file(path, poll_s: float=0.25, timeout_s: float | None=None, from_start: bool=True, encoding: str='utf-8')
```

Yield complete lines from a file that another process is appending to.

`from_start` reads what is already there before following; set it False
to take only what arrives from now on. `timeout_s` is an **idle**
timeout -- give up after that long with no new bytes -- and `None`
follows forever, so a caller wanting a bounded run should pass a number
or break out of the loop.

The load-bearing detail is that a read can land in the middle of a
line, and a half-line parsed as a sample is a wrong number rather than
an error. So bytes accumulate in `buf` and only text up to the last
newline is ever yielded; a trailing fragment waits for the rest of
itself. The final fragment of a file that stops without a newline is
discarded rather than guessed at.

#### `tcp_lines`

```python
tcp_lines(host: str, port: int, timeout_s: float | None=30.0, connect_timeout_s: float=10.0, encoding: str='utf-8')
```

Connect to `host:port` and yield complete lines until the peer closes.

`timeout_s` is the idle timeout on the socket; `None` blocks forever.
Same partial-line rule as `tail_file`, for the same reason -- TCP is a
byte stream and has no opinion about where a sample ends.

Reconnection is deliberately **not** here. A reconnect loses an unknown
number of samples, and a source that quietly papers over that gap hands
the estimator a record whose timebase is wrong in a way nothing
downstream can see. Catch the exception, note the outage, and start a
new stream on a new epoch.

#### `udp_lines`

```python
udp_lines(port: int, host: str='127.0.0.1', timeout_s: float | None=30.0, encoding: str='utf-8')
```

Bind a UDP port and yield lines from the datagrams arriving on it.

One datagram may hold several lines and, in principle, part of one --
so the same buffering applies. What UDP does *not* give you is order or
delivery, and neither is recoverable here: a lost datagram is a lost
sample, and a reordered one is refused downstream by `on_grid` rather
than sorted into place. That refusal is the right behaviour. Silently
sorting would mean the record's timebase came from the network's
scheduling rather than from the instrument.
